passage:
Warden's note, hostel B, Wednesday night. Jagdish knocked on my door at ten, phone in hand. He had sent a message to his friend Imtiaz at lunch about the group assignment and there had been no reply for eight hours. "I keep thinking he is angry about the presentation," he said. I asked what he could do with the worry other than carry it around. He thought for a minute, then typed, "Hey, are you annoyed with me, or am I imagining it? No pressure to reply fast." He showed me before sending. Imtiaz answered in minutes: his phone had been charging in the lab. Jagdish laughed, read the reply twice and went back to his room.
Mahima, hostel warden

qa.q: How long had Jagdish waited for a reply from Imtiaz?
qa.a: Jagdish had waited about eight hours with no reply.

qa.q: What was Jagdish afraid of when knocking on the warden's door?
qa.a: Jagdish was afraid that Imtiaz was angry about the presentation. The worry had built up over eight hours of silence.

qa.q: What did Jagdish do instead of building a story from the silence?
qa.a: Jagdish asked Imtiaz directly whether he was annoyed or imagining it, and added that there was no pressure to reply fast. The gentle, direct question ended the worry.

qa.q: What might Imtiaz have seen when the question arrived?
qa.a: Imtiaz may have seen a kind, honest message from a friend who cared, with room to answer. Imtiaz had only left the phone charging in the lab.

grounding: A young adult asks a friend directly and gently whether the friend is upset, rather than building a story from a delayed reply.

passage:
9:40 pm. My friend Sangeeta has not answered my message since morning. I only asked whether she would join the study group on Friday. By noon I had decided she was tired of me. By four I had a whole story: I talked too much last week, I forgot to thank her for the notes, she is pulling away. My chest hurt at dinner, and I barely tasted the food.
Then I thought, that is a lot of story for zero facts. So I wrote, "Hey, I have not heard from you and my brain is spinning. Are you cross with me, or is this just my imagination? 🙂"
She replied in five minutes: cousin's wedding, no signal all day. Sorry! Friday yes.
I feel silly and light. Note to self: ask sooner.
— Nilesh

qa.q: When did Nilesh write this diary entry?
How was Nilesh feeling by four o'clock and what shows it?
qa.a: Nilesh felt anxious and hurt, sure that Sangeeta was pulling away. The whole story about talking too much and forgetting to thank her for the notes shows the worry spiralling.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do that stopped the spiral?
qa.a: Nilesh noticed the story had zero facts and asked Sangeeta directly whether she was upset or if it was imagination. The question got an answer within five minutes.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta's day like before the reply?
qa.a: Sangeeta was at a cousin's wedding with no signal all day, so had no chance to answer. It had nothing to do with the study group or with Nilesh.

grounding: A young adult asks directly and gently whether a friend is upset instead of building a story from a delayed reply.
